prompt.context: Our client is in the energy business and makes electricity. The CEO is deciding on making a capital investment to expand capacity. How should we advise him?
prompt.question: Should the client make the $100M capital investment to expand electricity generation capacity, and how long would it take to pay back?

clarifying_info.q: How large is the investment and what capacity does it add?
clarifying_info.a: $100M investment to produce 2,000 units/week (units are Megawatts of electricity).

clarifying_info.q: What type of generators does the client use?
clarifying_info.a: The client uses natural gas fired generators.
Variable costs are gas and labor: gas costs $40/unit and labor is $10/unit.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market price of electricity?

framework: Assess the investment cost and capacity added (fixed cost structure)
Identify variable costs (natural gas, labor, distribution)
Calculate revenue potential at full capacity utilization
Calculate contribution margin and weekly/annual profit
Determine payback period and compare to useful life and industry benchmarks
Perform sensitivity analysis on demand and capacity utilization
Assess demand drivers and market trends
Evaluate competitive dynamics and potential pricing pressure

questions.prompt: What are the fixed costs involved in the investment?
questions.guidance: The $100M is the fixed capital investment to build capacity for 2,000 units/week. Candidate should identify this as the key fixed cost to recover.

questions.prompt: What are the variable costs for producing electricity?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the major variable cost buckets: natural gas, labor, and distribution/grid connection. The interviewer confirms gas at $40/unit and labor at $10/unit, totaling $50/unit in variable costs.

math.setup: Variable cost per unit = gas + labor

questions.prompt: Calculate the weekly and annual profit assuming full capacity utilization. What is the payback period?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate revenue, subtract variable costs to get contribution margin/profit, then divide the investment by annual profit to find payback period.

math.setup: Revenue = units/week * price/unit; Variable Cost = units/week * variable cost/unit; Profit = Revenue - Variable Cost; Payback = Investment / Annual Profit

questions.prompt: How would you evaluate whether this is an appropriate investment given the 20-year payback period?
questions.guidance: Compare payback period to the useful life of the plant (given as ~30 years) and to industry/company benchmarks. The interviewer confirms similar investments have payback periods of 15-20 years, so this is in-line.

questions.prompt: What else should you consider in assessing this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should raise sensitivity analysis on demand (the 100% capacity utilization assumption), and consider what happens if there is insufficient demand to fill the new capacity.

questions.prompt: How would you estimate new demand for electricity?
questions.guidance: Demand drivers include: new home starts, business/industrial growth, growth in consumer devices (white goods), offset by trends toward energy-efficient/low-energy appliances. Also assess competitor capacity expansions and their impact on pricing ability.

brainstorming.prompt: What trends or areas would you look at when assessing demand and market risk for this investment?

categories.name: Demand drivers
ideas: Business growth and new industrial complexes
Growth in consumer devices using electricity (white goods, electronics)

categories.name: Demand headwinds
ideas: Conservation trends and government efficiency mandates

categories.name: Competitive dynamics
ideas: Impact of competitor supply on market pricing power
Potential for price compression if market becomes oversupplied

recommendation: Recommend proceeding with the $100M investment: the ~20-year payback period is within the 15-20 year range of comparable investments and well within the plant's ~30-year useful life.
risks: The analysis assumes 100% capacity utilization; if demand is insufficient to fill new capacity, payback extends significantly
Competitor capacity additions could compress the $100/unit market price, eroding the contribution margin
Move toward energy-efficient appliances could dampen long-term demand growth
next_steps: Conduct sensitivity analysis on capacity utilization rates (e.g., 70%, 80%) to stress-test the payback period
Model demand growth scenarios using home starts, industrial growth, and appliance efficiency trends
Monitor competitor investment plans and assess their impact on regional electricity pricing
